d1-1.ev: The night drop scatters paratroopers across the countryside around this chiefly 82nd Airborne town.

q.t: Whose story is Sainte-Mère-Église chiefly?
q.x: Sainte-Mère-Église is chiefly an 82nd Airborne story; for Easy it shows the scale of the night-drop chaos.

d1-1.rem: The lesson here is dispersion: the night drop scattered men far from where they were meant to land.

d1-2.ev: Overloaded C-47s carry paratroopers through darkness and flak toward the drop zones.

q.t: Which aircraft does the museum use to explain what a 'stick' meant?
q.x: The C-47 and the 101st interpretation make this the best place to understand what a 'stick' meant.

d1-2.rem: Before any Easy man touched French soil there were overloaded aircraft, darkness, flak, jump lights and landing alone.

d1-3.ev: Winters lands west of Sainte-Mère-Église, separated from his company and without his weapon.

q.t: How did Winters arrive on the ground?
o: Separated from his company and without his weapon
By glider on the drop zone
q.x: Winters came down well off DZ C, separated from his company and without his weapon, then gathered scattered paratroopers.

d1-3.rem: This is a probable landing sector, not a surveyed point; the absence of a monument is part of the experience.

d1-4.ev: Easy men land across a broad area and assemble in improvised groups.

q.t: What does this stop show about the men of Sticks 68–71?
o: They landed across a broad area
They landed together on DZ C
q.x: Men landed across a broad area and assembled in improvised groups; the company that fought on 6 June was not the one that boarded in England.

d1-4.rem: The company that fought on 6 June was not the one that boarded in England.

d1-5.ev: C-47 42-93095, carrying Lt. Meehan and Easy paratroopers, is hit by flak and crashes.
d1-5.rem: All five aircrew and 17 paratroopers, among them Lt. Meehan and 1st Sgt. Evans, were killed here.

d1-6.ev: A separated Easy group of Guth, Talbert, Gordon and Tipper fights local actions nearby.

q.t: Who formed the separated Easy group linked to this area?
q.x: Guth, Talbert, 'Smokey' Gordon and Tipper were one of the small groups formed from whoever was nearby.

d1-6.rem: On D-Day small groups formed from whoever was nearby, fought local actions and moved toward friendly objectives.

d1-7.ev: Easy and 2/506 operate through the village after Brécourt as airborne and seaborne forces consolidate.

q.t: What role does Sainte-Marie-du-Mont play in the 506th's D-Day story?
o: The heart of its D-Day sector
q.x: Sainte-Marie-du-Mont was the heart of the 506th's D-Day sector, linking the landings, the routes to Utah and the Brécourt action.

d1-7.rem: Here the scattered story of the night drop converges; the church tower is your geographic reset.

d1-8.ev: Winters reaches the battalion CP and receives the mission that leads to Brécourt.

q.t: Why was Winters drawn into leadership here?
o: He was promoted before the jump
q.x: With Meehan missing, Winters was drawn into the leadership vacuum and sent to neutralize artillery firing toward Utah Beach.

d1-8.rem: This is the hinge of the story: the leadership vacuum that put Winters in charge of the Brécourt assault.

d1-9.ev: Junior officers such as Winters take the lead on D-Day in the bocage near Utah.

q.t: What does the Winters monument represent?
o: The junior officers who led on D-Day
q.x: The monument stands for the junior officers who led on D-Day; it is not a combat position.

d1-9.rem: Winters stands here for all the junior officers who led on D-Day, on the road to Utah Beach.

d1-10.ev: Easy men attack the battery whose guns are believed to be firing toward Utah Beach.

q.t: Where were the Brécourt guns believed to be firing?
q.x: The guns were believed to be firing toward Utah Beach; the memorial is the public viewpoint over the private battery area.

d1-10.rem: The memorial identifies the men who took part; the battery ground itself is private, so read it from here.

d1-11.ev: Lt. Winters leads a small Easy force against the four guns at Brécourt Manor.

q.t: How did Winters's force take the guns?
o: One frontal charge across open ground
In sequence, via the connecting trench
q.x: Under suppressive fire, small groups got into the trench and took the four guns one by one; the force then withdrew rather than assaulting the manor.

d1-11.rem: Four guns were taken one by one from a connecting trench; the exact position of every gun pit is still debated.

d1-12.ev: Troops and vehicles come ashore through a vulnerable beachhead while airborne troops secure exits inland.

q.t: What do the museum's maps explain about Brécourt?
o: Why artillery threatened the beach exits
q.x: Its maps of beach exits and artillery threats make clear why guns firing toward Utah had to be silenced.

d1-12.rem: The beach and the airborne drop were two halves of one plan: the airborne secured the exits the beach depended on.

d1-13.ev: Easy Company moves down to Utah Beach to embark, ending its Normandy campaign.

q.t: How does Easy's Normandy campaign end at Utah Beach?
o: It holds the dunes against a counterattack
q.x: Easy jumped inland rather than landing here, but its Normandy campaign ended on this beach with embarkation on 10–11 July.

d1-13.rem: Utah, the westernmost landing beach, depended on forces inland, and it was from here that Easy left Normandy in July.

d2-1.ev: The 82nd Airborne fights for the Merderet crossings in some of the invasion's fiercest airborne combat.

q.t: What made the La Fière causeway so hard to fight over?
o: Flooded lowlands turned the road into a bottleneck
q.x: Flooded lowlands turned the causeway into a bottleneck; the same problem returns on the approach to Carentan.

d2-1.rem: Control of a single causeway over flooded ground could decide a battle, a lesson repeated on the way to Carentan.

d2-2.ev: The 506th takes the village while Easy is held in reserve.

q.t: Where was Easy when the 506th took St-Côme-du-Mont on 8 June?
q.x: The 506th took the village on 8 June while Easy was in reserve; hedgerows and narrow roads fragmented every movement.

d2-2.rem: Short map distances concealed difficult ground: every hedge a wall, every junction an objective.

d2-3.ev: Easy passes the crossroads moving south toward Carentan.

q.t: Which link to Easy's D-Day losses has been displayed at this museum?
q.x: Material from Lt. Meehan's crashed C-47 has been displayed here; Easy itself passed this corner on the evening of 11 June.

d2-3.rem: This was not Easy's battle site; the company passed the corner on the evening of 11 June on its way to Carentan.

d2-4.ev: Easy crosses the Douve causeway corridor, then leaves the road for the fields.

q.t: What dictated movement in the Douve sector?
q.x: Waterways, marshes, bridges and raised roads left few alternatives, so a junction or causeway mattered far beyond its size.

d2-4.rem: In low wet fields with few routes, possession of a junction or causeway mattered far beyond its size on a map.

d2-5.ev: Troops advancing along the causeway are exposed, with marsh either side and no room to manoeuvre.

q.t: Whose story is Purple Heart Lane chiefly?
q.x: It is chiefly a 502nd PIR story, but it is the battlefield Easy moved into on the way to Carentan.

d2-5.rem: On a narrow causeway with marsh on both sides, men advancing toward Carentan had no room to manoeuvre.

d2-6.ev: Easy fights building to building along Rue Holgate toward the railway, where Winters is wounded.

q.t: Where was Winters wounded in Carentan?
o: In the shin near the railway
In the arm at the church
q.x: Easy fought building to building toward the railway, where Winters was wounded in the shin; the company was then billeted here 13–19 June.

d2-6.rem: Carentan was the prize between the Utah and Omaha lodgements, and Easy fought its way in on 12 June.

d2-7.ev: German forces counterattack south-west of Carentan; the 506th holds until armour arrives.

q.t: What was Easy's task at Bloody Gulch on 13 June?
q.x: German forces counterattacked and the 506th held until armour from the 2nd Armored Division helped restore the situation. The exact hedgerow line is disputed.

d2-7.rem: For Easy, Bloody Gulch was a test of holding ground rather than seizing it.

d3-1.ev: The German dead of the Normandy fighting are laid to rest here.
d3-1.rem: A place of remembrance for the German dead, widening the story from one unit to the human cost of the war.

d3-2.ev: Rangers make their cliff assault across ground cratered by the pre-invasion bombardment.

q.t: How does Pointe du Hoc relate to Brécourt?
o: The same kind of threat, on a larger scale
q.x: The Rangers' cliff assault was separate from Easy's, but it faced the same kind of threat as Brécourt, on a larger scale.

d3-2.rem: The preserved craters and casemates make the pre-invasion bombardment legible; the landscape itself is the exhibit.

d3-3.ev: Troops land on open sand beneath commanding bluffs, with few exits off the beach.

q.t: What made Dog Green one of Omaha's most punishing sectors?
o: Open sand, few exits, commanding bluffs
q.x: Open sand, limited exits and commanding bluffs; the contrast with Utah explains why the two beachheads developed so differently.

d3-3.rem: The exposure is the lesson: open sand beneath commanding bluffs, with few ways off the beach.

d3-4.ev: Along this frontage the draws are the only routes off the beach, overlooked by the bluffs.

q.t: On Omaha, what were the 'draws'?
q.x: The draws were the routes off the beach; comparing exits, bluffs and fields of fire across the frontage shows how the fight was shaped.

d3-4.rem: What mattered on Omaha was not shoreline distance but the draws that led off the beach.

d3-5.ev: Above Omaha Beach, the battlefield becomes individual loss.
d3-5.rem: Its place above Omaha makes geography and remembrance inseparable; each marker is an individual life.

d3-6.ev: The whole Normandy campaign unfolds: bocage, attrition, breakout and collapse.

q.t: What does the Bayeux museum add to Easy's story?
q.x: It widens the lens from 6 June to the whole campaign, so Easy's story can be placed within the bocage, attrition and breakout.

d3-6.rem: Easy's weeks in Normandy were one part of a much larger campaign of bocage fighting, attrition and breakout.

d4-1.ev: The Atlantic Wall works as an artillery system, its guns set in spaced casemates.

q.t: What survives at Longues-sur-Mer?
q.x: Original guns remain in their casemates, making it one of the best places to understand the Atlantic Wall as a working artillery system.

d4-1.rem: The spacing between positions is part of the system: this was a battery, not a single bunker.

d4-2.ev: Port Winston lets men, vehicles and supplies flow into Normandy.

q.t: What was the Mulberry harbour for?
q.x: Port Winston let men, vehicles and supplies flow into Normandy through offshore caissons, floating roadways and shore discharge.

d4-2.rem: The harbour is best read as a system, offshore caissons to floating roadways to shore, across the whole bay.

d4-3.ev: Above Gold Beach, British and Commonwealth sacrifice in a coalition invasion is remembered.
d4-3.rem: The names here turn numbers back into individuals; Overlord was a coalition operation.

d5-1.ev: The museum sets D-Day and the Battle of Normandy within the war's origins, occupation and course.

q.t: What is the Caen Memorial's role on this tour?
o: The strategic frame for the whole war
q.x: It gives the strategic frame, from the war's origins through occupation, D-Day and the Battle of Normandy, after four days of terrain.

d5-1.rem: Placed after four days of terrain, the museum frames the war as a whole, including the civilian experience.

d5-2.ev: British glider troops capture the Orne and canal bridges in a precise opening action.

q.t: How did the Pegasus Bridge action differ from the American drop?
q.x: The glider capture was one of D-Day's most precise opening actions, the opposite of the scattered American drop.

d5-2.rem: Opposite in execution to the scattered American drop, but with the same aim: secure crossings and protect a flank.

d5-3.ev: The 9th Parachute Battalion attacks the battery despite severe dispersal and lost equipment.

q.t: Which unit attacked the Merville Battery?
q.x: The 9th Parachute Battalion attacked despite severe dispersal and lost equipment, the direct parallel to Brécourt.

d5-3.rem: Merville is the direct parallel to Brécourt: a battery attacked by dispersed paratroopers, readable here from the defender's side.

x-ang.ev: Two 101st medics, Wright and Moore, treat wounded of both sides inside the church.

q.t: What did medics Wright and Moore do in this church?
o: Held it as a sniper post
q.x: The church became an airborne aid station where Wright and Moore treated wounded of both sides; the bloodstained pews survive.

x-ang.rem: The bloodstained pews survive from the days when two medics treated the wounded of both sides here.

x-vie.ev: Easy leads the 2nd Battalion column on point and meets German paratroopers.

q.t: Whom did Easy meet on point at Vierville on 7 June?
q.x: Leading the 2nd Battalion column, Easy met German paratroopers; the village was cleared with support from other 506th elements and armour.

x-vie.rem: Easy led the battalion here on 7 June; this is the Cotentin Vierville, not Vierville-sur-Mer at Omaha.

x-nvm.ev: Hedgerow fighting shapes the daily life of soldiers and civilians in the bocage.

q.t: Which part of Easy's Normandy experience does this museum cover best?
q.x: It is strong on the bocage battle that followed Carentan, the world Easy lived in from 13 to 28 June.

x-nvm.rem: From 13 to 28 June Easy lived in the hedgerow world shown here, among soldiers and civilians alike.

x-bgm.ev: The 13 June counterattack that Easy helps repel is told on the ground where it happened.

q.t: Which event does this museum focus on?
q.x: The museum tells the fighting after Carentan, including the 13 June counterattack Easy helped repel, on the ground where it happened.

x-bgm.rem: It tells the 13 June counterattack from the ground where Easy helped repel it.

x-ddw.ev: Aircraft and crews carry the airborne divisions and cover the beaches.

q.t: What is the D-Day Wings Museum's focus?
o: Aviation: the aircraft and their crews
q.x: It gives aviation context: the aircraft and crews that carried the airborne divisions and covered the beaches.

x-ddw.rem: Every airborne soldier depended on the aircraft and crews that carried him to Normandy.

dd-0.ev: A heavy 210 mm naval battery duels with the fleet off Utah until taken on 12 June.

q.t: When was the Crisbecq Battery finally taken?
q.x: The heavy 210 mm battery dueled with the fleet off Utah and was not taken until 12 June.

dd-0.rem: The Brécourt battery was a small cousin of heavy naval guns like these.

dd-1.ev: Four tunnel-linked casemates, painted to look like houses, fire on Utah.

q.t: How were Azeville's casemates disguised?
q.x: Its four casemates, linked by tunnels, were painted to look like houses; the battery fired on Utah and held out until 9 June.

dd-1.rem: The battery held out until 9 June, firing on Utah from casemates disguised as houses.

dd-2.ev: The Canadians take heavy first-hour losses, then advance further inland than any other force.

q.t: What distinguished the Canadians on Juno on D-Day?
q.x: They took the heaviest losses of the British beaches in the first hour, then advanced further inland than any other force on D-Day.

dd-2.rem: After the heaviest first-hour losses of the British beaches, the Canadians went further inland than any other force on D-Day.

dd-3.ev: Canadian dead from Juno and the fighting for Caen are laid to rest here.
dd-3.rem: 2,048 Canadians from Juno and the fighting for Caen rest here, in a quiet and rarely crowded cemetery.

dd-4.ev: The German regimental HQ bunker holds up the Suffolks for most of D-Day.

q.t: What did the Hillman strongpoint help stop?
q.x: The German regimental HQ bunker complex held up the Suffolks for most of D-Day and helped stop Sword's advance on Caen.

dd-4.rem: One bunker complex could delay a whole beachhead: Hillman helped stop the advance on Caen.

dd-5.ev: Lord Lovat's commandos land with a piper playing and march to relieve Pegasus Bridge.

q.t: Where did Lovat's commandos march after landing?
q.x: Lord Lovat's commandos landed with a piper playing and marched to relieve Pegasus Bridge by early afternoon.

dd-5.rem: Lovat's commandos landed here to a piper's tune and reached Pegasus Bridge by early afternoon.

dd-6.ev: Men of the British 6th Airborne are buried beside the first village liberated by the British.
dd-6.rem: 2,236 graves, mostly of the airborne division, lie beside the first village liberated by the British.
